title: Winter Arc 2025 is CANCELLED
summary: NH criticizes the 'winter arc' trend as a symptom of commodified online self-improvement: it relies on borrowed motivation and group hype, and its three-month window breeds PR chasing and dropouts. Drawing on Debord's Society of the Spectacle, he argues fitness has become something people watch rather than do, and that real change needs a year-round habit, physically earned confidence and a personal 'why'.
claims: Young men wanting to self-improve is good; the problem is that modern self-improvement culture now promotes mediocrity instead of excellence
Self-improvement pushes cluster in the cold months and around New Year because people see them as a fresh start; this always existed, social media just repackaged and hyped it
Needing a winter arc means waiting for an arbitrary signal; if you really wanted to change you would start immediately
Three months is barely the first step; instead of a winter arc you need a year-round arc
His gym manager says that of 100 people who buy a yearly membership, about 20 still train two months later and maybe 5 after four to six months
People who finish a winter arc and keep the habits gain consistency and discipline, which already makes them exceptional
Many men in France say they have lifted for 5-10 years but their physiques don't show it: they started 10 years ago and keep repeating the same three fruitless months
Losing progress is easier than gaining it; days of grind are undone by a period of inactivity
External motivation is never sustainable; motivation content fills people with empty motivation and keeps them from building discipline
Sigma and alpha motivation edits preach self-reliance to people who need group hype just to get to the gym
Goggins preaches self-motivation yet got rich motivating others; hiring him or watching motivation videos is outsourcing your motivation, paid with money or time
His own transformation was a two-month self-motivated summer arc that changed him body and soul
At 16-17 he could only get up at 6 a.m. to run by playing a motivational clip; his mother asked whether he was a puppet without willpower, which made him see his dependence
If you can only train when hyped on pre-workout or caffeine, your relationship with training is compromised; it's fine to start that way but not as a crutch
The most important part of self-improvement is finding your why; 'because it's my winter arc' is circular and disappears when the arc ends
Gurus leave out the spiritual side of self-improvement because it can't be sold
Teenagers are most receptive to peer pressure and risk downloading a personality online instead of finding their own
Manosphere influencers are the male equivalent of makeup influencers: they create clones who chase a downgraded image of themselves built on possessions
Under capitalism self-improvement becomes a commodity and a Ponzi scheme; gurus get rich by selling the grind, and an ineffective product sells even better
He defines confidence as the innate belief that you will be okay whatever happens, which carries over to approaching women or attempting a 5-rep max
Confidence is physical: it comes from actually achieving things and cannot be downloaded through motivational content
A good habit-building video should essentially tell you to turn it off and go do the thing; excellence is built by doing it always
Consumption is about forgetting yourself, while self-improvement should mean spending time with yourself; he recommends Debord's Society of the Spectacle, ideally in French
Winter arcs encourage PR culture: chasing heavier weights at the expense of technique and volume, a mistake intermediate and advanced lifters recognize
A three-month window pushes beginners to chase numbers like +40 kg on the squat, which leads to injury or plateaus; lifting is a marathon where the tortoise beats the hare
Teens shown blowing up during a winter arc are genetic freaks or on drugs, and comparing to them kills your enthusiasm
Fitness on social media has become a spectator sport: online standards are 240 lb with 20-inch arms while real young men get weaker, and he is often the biggest guy in his gym
Gurus benefit when you stay small, weak and undisciplined because you keep consuming their content
